title: NXP reportedly in talks to acquire vehicle chip supplier Ambarella
teaser: NXP may acquire Ambarella, gaining powerful chips vital for L4 autonomous vehicles.
summary: NXP Semiconductors is reportedly in talks to acquire Ambarella Inc., a key rival supplier of advanced vehicle chips. The acquisition would significantly bolster NXP's presence in the burgeoning autonomous and ADAS markets. Ambarella's technology, such as its CV3-AD685 chip, enables L4 autonomy—allowing vehicles to operate without driver input in most situations. This specialized chip features a safety island for critical code and utilizes algorithms like Oculii (for radar data processing) that help process complex environmental data collected from car sensors, crucial for self-driving cars.
author: Maria Deutscher
content: NXP Semiconductors NV is reportedly in talks to buy Ambarella Inc., a fellow provider of vehicle chips. The Financial Times today cited sources as saying that other industry players could also make bids. The report didn't divulge any other details, notably what sale price Ambarella is seeking. The company had a market capitalization of about $3.25 billion before the acquisition rumors boosted its shares by 16%. Any bids the company receives will likely value it higher. Netherlands-based NXP is among the world's largest suppliers of car chips. Its processors can be found in infotainment devices, autonomous driving systems and a variety of other auto parts. NXP is also active in several additional segments including the data center market. Its chips are used for tasks such as distributing electricity to servers and managing the flow of coolant. Santa Clara, California-based Ambarella competes in many of the same segments as NXP, most notably the auto sector. The company makes chips that enable carmakers to install artificial intelligence software in their vehicles. Ambarella debuted its newest auto chip in January. The CV7 combines a four-core central processing unit with an image signal processor and a video encoder. The image signal processor enhances footage from the host vehicle's sensors by removing errors, boosting brightness and performing other edits. The CV7's video encoder, in turn, compresses footage into a memory-efficient format that can be more easily sent over the network. The chip also features an artificial intelligence accelerator. According to Ambarella, the module is based on a custom architecture that can provide five times better power-efficiency than competing designs. The technology enables the CV7 to run transformer-based language models. Carmakers can use the chip to power their vehicles' ADAS, or advanced driver assistance systems. Such modules provided limited autonomy features such as automated parking and lane centering. Ambarella offers the CV7 alongside a more advanced processor called the CV3-AD685. It can equip vehicles with L4 autonomy, or the ability to operate without driver input in most situations. The chip features a hardened processing module called a safety island that is optimized to run the host car's most sensitive code. Many autonomous vehicles enrich footage from their cameras with radar measurements. Radar sensors work by transmitting radio waves and measuring how they're reflected by nearby objects. Each reflected radio wave becomes a dot in a point cloud, a three-dimensional map of the car's environment. The CV3-AD685 ships with a set of radar algorithms called Oculii. According to Ambarella, the software adapts the radio waves generated by a car's radars to the environment in which they operate. That reduces the number of antennas needed to collect radar data while boosting mapping resolution. Ambarella's technology could help NXP boost its presence in the autonomous vehicle market. Waymo LLC, Amazon.com Inc.'s Zoox unit and other industry players are currently in the process of growing their self-driving taxi fleets. Ambarella's chips are also used in more than a half-dozen other segments including the industrial robot market. title: xAI adds character references and 1080p to Imagine Video 1.5
teaser: xAI just supercharged its video AI: Imagine Video 1.5 now handles native 1080p output and maintains consistent characters/voices across scenes using references.
summary: xAI has significantly upgraded Imagine Video 1.5, enhancing video creation with advanced controls like multi-references and voice continuity. The update allows users to shape clips not just through text prompts but also by supplying reference images and voice samples for tighter identity control. Key features include native 1080p generation and Multi-Reference, which accepts up to seven distinct visual anchors—allowing creators to keep a character while changing the scene or vice versa. Most notably, 'Voice consistency' ensures that the model can maintain both the face and the voice of a recurring character across multiple generated shots, addressing a major need in production.
author: Alexey Shabanov
content: xAI has expanded Imagine Video 1.5 with image and voice references, prompt-only video generation, and native 1080p output. The update gives users several ways to shape a clip: describe a shot without a starting image, guide it with reference images, or combine a character image with a voice sample. Image and voice references are starting in the United States for SuperGrok Heavy and SuperGrok Plus subscribers on Grok's Imagine website and iOS app. xAI says the tools will roll out to all tiers over the next few days. Text-to-video and native 1080p generation are already generally available through Grok Imagine on the web, iOS, and Android, with 1080p supported for both text-to-video and image-to-video workflows. Multi-Reference lets creators assign separate visual anchors to a generation. One image can hold a face in place, another can preserve a product, and another can define a location. Users can keep a character while changing the scene, retain a scene while swapping the character, or preserve both while altering only the action. The model accepts up to seven references in a single generation. Voice consistency adds another layer of continuity. When a character image and voice reference are supplied together, xAI says the model can maintain the same face and voice across scenes. That targets a common production need: generating multiple shots around a recurring character without rebuilding identity cues for every clip. Developers can access image references, text-to-video, and native 1080p through the xAI API using the grok-imagine-video-1.5 model. Voice references require a request to xAI. The API example shows a prompt, reference image URL, duration, aspect ratio, and resolution passed into a video generation call. The rollout extends the Imagine Video 1.5 release introduced last month, which xAI presented as an advance in motion, physics, and audio. The latest additions shift the focus toward tighter control over identity, scene, and product while expanding the model from image-led animation to videos generated directly from text. Source

title: The OG reading app just got a big update
teaser: From reading apps (Instapaper's big redesign) to AI email clients (Sunflower) and Markdown editors (Emerald), here is a tech deep dive into essential productivity tools.
summary: In this comprehensive tech digest, the major highlight is Instapaper's robust relaunch, featuring a redesign and improved web app that solidifies its place as a top-tier read-later service. The article also reviewed several other valuable productivity tools. For Mac users, Pastebot 3 offers enhanced clipboard management. Developers can use Emerald, a new Markdown editor solving collaboration pain points on Apple devices. Furthermore, the piece details Sunflower, an advanced email client incorporating helpful AI features like in-built summarizing and chat capabilities for managing your inbox.
author: David Pierce
content: Hi, friends! Welcome to Installer No. 138, your guide to the best and Verge -iest stuff in the world. (If you're new here, welcome, happy August, and also you can read all the old editions at the Installer homepage .) This week, I've been reading about microwave sounds and Meta glasses and Alex vs. Alix , testing the Logitech Alto Keys K98M to see if I'm ready for the mechanical keyboard life, digging into the history of the first chatbot , clearing space on my desk for a Bob Ross deskmat , doing a full Ted Lasso rewatch ahead of the new season next week, finally getting into Cyberpunk 2077 now that it's so cheap, cackling and nodding at this Adobe hate post , and upgrading my home camera setup with the truly enormous Elgato Prompter XL . Also, I have some personal news: I'm having a baby! (If your response to this is, Didn't you just have like 37 other babies , yes, yes I did. Pray for me.) I'm planning to be out from about mid-August to the beginning of October, but I'm also in could-happen-anytime land now. So if I'm suddenly gone, that's why! Just like last year, my colleague Jay Peters will be taking over Installer while I'm out, and just like last year, he's going to be great. But for now, I'm still here! I also have for you a new superhero movie, a new take on an old game, some great Musk-related comedy, and much more. Let's do it. (As always, the best part of Installer is your ideas and tips. What are you watching / reading / playing / listening to / putting in a blender this week? Tell me everything: installer@theverge.com . And if you know someone else who might enjoy Installer , forward it to them and tell them to subscribe here .) Spider-Man: Brand New Day . The Tom Holland Spidey era just never seems to miss. It's pretty impressive to pull off a more or less full story reboot while keeping all the same actors and characters, but by all accounts this one pulls it off. Since I still can't get IMAX Odyssey tickets, this one's at the top of my to-watch list. Pastebot 3 . Missed this one last week! Great clipboard managers are right up there with launchers and text expanders in the "how did I ever use a computer without this" category, and Pastebot is one of the Mac's best. The new version has smart organization options, support for all kinds of media, and much more. The kind of app you'll find new uses for... forever. President Curtis . I was going to describe this as "basically a Rick and Morty spinoff" before I realized it's actually a Rick and Morty spinoff. Perhaps unsurprisingly, people seem to either love it or hate it. I think most of us would agree R&M is not what it once was, but the idea of throwing all its chaotic energy into the US government does pay off at least a few times. And it's not not political commentary, you know? " Why Is So Much AI Tech Useless? " Two of my favorite people on the internet - Joanna Stern and Hasan Minhaj - go deep on where AI is, and isn't, actually good and useful in our lives. Minhaj's complete disbelief at all these overhyped products just gives me life. Halo: Campaign Evolved . Confession: I was always terrible at Halo , and I've always been unfairly mad at the series because of it. The new remake appears to be a mediocre game (with terrible dialogue) but great nostalgia bait, and that might be enough for a lot of people looking to get Master Chief back into their lives. Leafy Corner . This game exists somewhere on the spectrum between Animal Crossing and RollerCoaster Tycoon, and I mean both as a compliment. It's a quiet, cozy game, but also something of a management sim, all in the confines of a plant shop. Adorable. Spotify Running Mode . I actually think Spotify's last take on running, with adaptive tempos and generative beats, was both cooler and a more interesting take on AI. But Spotify's prompted playlists have generally been pretty good, and I appreciate having the timing updates built in instead of having some other app constantly ducking my music to tell me I'm too slow. " Elon's Epic Ego Explained . " Nobody does topical comedy like Josh Johnson, and this is my favorite of his recent sets. It's not just 45 minutes of making fun of Musk - it's also about The Odyssey and a bunch of other things - but it's both ruthless and right about the world's richest man. The SwitchBot Battery Circulator Fan 2 Pro . My colleague Thomas Ricker has successfully convinced me that SwitchBot's fans are worth a look over the "whatever's on the shelf at Target" models I've been buying for years. This new $120 model is quiet and powerful, charges over USB-C, and is going to live on my patio the rest of the summer. I buried the lede here: The biggest new thing of the week, at least in my book, is Instapaper 10 . Instapaper is one of the original read-later apps, and has continued to be among the best on the market. After some weird ownership stuff over the years, Instapaper has been in the hands of Brian Donohue, who has been steadily improving the service in lots of ways. This week's launch comes with a really nice redesign, a way better web app, and a lot of helpful organization and reading tools. I've been testing it, and I think it's back to being my go-to recommendation for reading apps. (For power users I still think Readwise is the move.) With the new app out, I asked Brian to share his homescreen with us - I wanted to see how he organized his stuff, and if he might be working on even more cool stuff. Turns out he is! Here's his homescreen, plus some info on the apps he uses and why: The phone: iPhone 16 Pro. I almost always purchase iPhones every other generation. Maybe a foldable this year ? The wallpaper: My daughter, as a reminder that my apps must be good otherwise she will not have food on the table. The apps: Safari, Google Calendar, Emerald, Google Maps, Weather, Photos, Instapaper, Kobo Books, Reddit, 1Password, Google Authenticator, Slack, Google Docs, Google Sheets, ForeFlight, Flight Circle, Claude, Linear, Phone, Sunflower, Messages, Spotify. I'll start with the ones not yet in the App Store: Emerald and Sunflower. Emerald is a Markdown editor I'm working on that solves two personal pain points: native iOS / macOS client, and collaboration on markdown files. I have been a big Obsidian user the past two years, but it's been failing me in those areas. I've been writing with Emerald exclusively for the past few months and it's almost ready for beta testing. Waitlist in the link. Sunflower is a new email client from Bobby Goodlatte and friends. It's beautifully designed and has some tasteful AI features, like summarizing your inbox, chatting with your email, and an Autopilot feature which seems to be perpetually "Coming Soon." I've been trying a few clients in the "AI email" space like Extra , and an autopilot tool called Cora , which didn't stick . Instapaper's big launch this week included a new home screen widget. It fits nicely in the widget stack alongside the Apple News, Stocks, and Weather widgets. Additionally, you have many of the usual suspects. I am doing a huge amount of my work with Claude and Linear these days, both of which have fantastic iOS apps. I also asked Brian to share a few things he's into right now. Here's what he sent back: I've always been inspired by creative builders, and two come to mind right now. The first is Andrew Jones , who has been building free & open-source alternatives to paid software (e.g. Granola , Wispr Flow ) - fingers crossed Instapaper is not next. The second is Q , a designer who has been building small, single-purpose websites for himself that I find inspiring. It almost reminds me of a purer, distant version of the Internet, where you built a bunch of Geocities pages for fun and without expectations of fame and fortune. Hyper Mesh . Q has been exploring image reveal animations, and built a tool to tweak presets on the initial mask and the animation that reveals the image. SVG Star Editor . Create a star from different settings and export to SVG. Chess Moves . Q is learning how to play chess with his girlfriend and made this tutorial website as a companion tool. Here's what the Installer community is into this week. I want to know what you're into right now as well! Email installer@theverge.com or message me on Signal - @davidpierce.11 - with your recommendations for anything and everything, and we'll feature some of our favorites here every week. For even more great recommendations, check out the replies to this post on Threads and this post on Bluesky. "I am hopelessly hooked on the game Murdoku . It's free online, or you can play old school through books . It's a logic game where you solve crimes by process of elimination." - Kurt "I've been loving Paradiso for finding movie showtimes. Not only does it alert you when something on your Letterboxd watchlist is playing near you, it also beats Fandango or other apps for simply browsing first run showtimes." - Mike "My friend recently ordered a Galaxy Z Fold 8 and I had to introduce them to Good Lock ." - B "I love Anker stuff and tend to choose it over everything else. But I have the Anker 3-in-1 travel charger and... this ESR one (a brand I hadn't really heard of) is the better product in every way. The Apple Watch charger is in a better place, it's thinner, and the cooling fan works better. I can't vouch for long-term reliability yet, but I have one by my bedside and one in my travel bag!" - Peter "Finally switched from a mess of read-it-later apps to a second brain with Obsidian + Claude , inspired by Karpathy's LLM Wiki concept. Hoping this setup is the one that actually sticks..." - Kartik "I use Readwise Reader for all my newsletters. It has unique email addresses to either add newsletters to your library or RSS feed. I love keeping all my things to read all in the same app, read later, newsletters, pdfs..." - Rich "HIGHLY recommend the movie Avatar Aang: The Last Airbender . It's a crime and shame that Paramount isn't putting this into more theaters, AND that the movie was leaked on X earlier this year. Amazing film with all-time stunning visuals that honestly left me angry I was watching it on TV at home. Deserves bettering than being dumped on Paramount Plus." - Nolan "Watching the restored version of Lawrence of Arabia . Peter O'Toole's blue eyes are dreamy." - SaltedPork The coolest internet experience I had this week was scrolling through the Everything Machine , a deep and detailed breakdown of how your phone works. It's only the first chapter of what I hope will be a very long exploration of how smartphones changed everything, and I love the way it seems to interact with your phone as you scroll. Our phones are such a "This is water" thing in our lives now, and I really enjoy anything that makes me pay a little more attention to the object, the cultural force, and the economic engine that takes up so much of my life. Highly recommend taking a scroll. Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates. David Pierce Gadgets Installer Streaming Tech

title: Apps that help you break free from doomscrolling and get active
teaser: Want to escape doomscrolling? Apps like MeBeMe assign 'missions' based on your identity instead of just blocking access!
summary: A wave of new apps is addressing the issue of addictive 'doomscrolling' by incentivizing physical activity and positive habit formation. While multiple tools exist, such as Digital Carrot (which uses GPS challenges) or StepBloc/Walkly (locking apps until step goals are met), MeBeMe stands out with its unique motivational approach. Instead of restricting access, MeBeMe assigns personalized 'missions' based on chosen user identities—like 'athlete' or 'historian.' Other innovative mechanics include TouchGrass, which requires photographing actual grass to unlock apps, and Steppin, which trades physical steps for screen time. These technologies offer users ways to consciously manage digital consumption while promoting real-world movement.
author: Lauren Forristal
content: Doomscrolling can be addictive. It's common to end up on the couch for hours, mindlessly scrolling through feeds, which inevitably messes up your posture and, in the end, just ends up making you feel bad about yourself. Your eyes definitely don't like it, either. Fortunately, there are several apps that encourage you to get up and move before you dive into social media. There's even one that literally has you go outside and touch grass before you can scroll TikTok or Instagram. So, if you're looking to cut back on screen time and be a little more active, here's a roundup of some apps that can help. Digital Carrot Image Credits: Digital Carrot Digital Carrot blocks distracting apps, websites and games until you meet your daily fitness, productivity or screen time goals. It connects to wearables like the Apple Watch, and you can set personalized targets, say walking 6,000 steps a day. It also supports GPS- and time-based challenges, allowing users to block apps until they spend a certain amount of time at a specific location, such as completing a 60-minute workout at the gym. The app's available on iPhone , Android , as well as macOS, Windows, and Linux. MeBeMe Image Credits: MeBeMe MeBeMe is aimed at helping users cultivate better habits. Instead of blocking phone access, the app sends you notifications to achieve certain missions, such as doing burpees, connecting with people, or warming up for three minutes. Though not solely focused on physical activity, its "Body" category includes challenges for athletes, dancers, cyclists, and runners. The app is currently available for free for iOS devices. StepBloc Image Credits: App Store StepBloc lets you lock access to apps until you walk a number of steps you can specify. In addition, you can also have link app access to completing specific workouts, such as push-ups, planks or squats for a specified amount of time. Once the workout is completed, the user can access selected apps like Instagram, TikTok, YouTube or games. This makes StepBloc particularly useful for people who want to offset their sedentary habits with short bursts of exercise. StepBloc is free on iOS devices , and requires a subscription for unlimited access. Steppin Image Credits: Steppin Created by the founder of Kayak, Steppin lets you trade physical movement for screen time. For example, it allows you to reward yourself with one minute of scrolling for every 100 steps you take. You have the flexibility to set your own step goals for accessing social media, streaming services or mobile games. It's available to download on iOS devices. TouchGrass Image Credits: TouchGrass TouchGrass brings a unique twist to preventing doomscrolling habits by requiring you to step outside and take a photo of grass to unlock distracting apps. The app uses computer vision models to scan photos, and it will only accept images of grass (not trees or other plants). The freemium version allows you to lock two apps, and you can pay $5.99 per month or $49.99 per year to be able to lock more apps. TouchGrass is available for iOS devices . WalkLock Image Credits: WalkLock This iOS app integrates with Apple Health to limit access to designated apps until you meet your daily step goal. The app automatically tracks steps using health data collected by the iPhone or Apple Watch. It offers a lockscreen widget, too, which displays progress throughout the day, making it easy to monitor how close you are to unlocking apps. Walkly Image Credits: Google Play Store Walkly is an Android app that provides a similar experience as WalkLock. It locks selected social media, gaming, and other distracting apps until users walk a predetermined number of steps. The app continuously monitors physical activity and automatically unlocks apps when the walking goal has been achieved. WeWard Image Credits: WeWard WeWard initially launched as an app that incentivized walking by awarding users "Wards," an in-app currency that can be exchanged for cash, gift cards or donations. It recently introduced "Walking Mode," which allows users to restrict app access until they meet specific step counts. Both the step goals and locked apps are customizable. It's available for iOS and Android .

title: This $9 key physically locks your most addictive apps
teaser: Autonomous Key is an NFC device that tackles digital addiction by physically locking apps—you need a scan, not just willpower.
summary: Introducing Autonomous Key, an NFC physical device designed to curb digital distractions by making accessing apps difficult. Instead of relying on willpower (like traditional screen-time limits), users must physically scan the key with their phone to unlock distracting apps for up to 60 minutes. For just $9, it is significantly cheaper than competitors like Blok ($29) or Brick ($59). The accompanying app adds value through AI insights, summarizing usage habits with a uniquely 'sassy' tone. While compact and compatible with Android 8.0+ and iOS 15+, the key requires a physical effort to bypass locks, turning impulse scrolling into a deliberate decision. It operates without required subscriptions.
author: Lauren Forristal
content: Screen-time apps aren't effective for many people because, in the end, they depend on your willpower. They remind you to stop scrolling or let you set timers, but such notifications can be easy to ignore. Autonomous Key takes a different approach to this issue simply by being a physical device. It's an NFC key that pairs with a companion app to let you lock away distracting apps. So instead of tapping a button to bypass the block, you have to physically scan the key with your phone to regain access to your locked apps. Each unlock session can last for up to 60 minutes before the apps are automatically locked again. That physical requirement is what makes the idea compelling. Instead of depending on your self-control, you can leave the NFC key in another room, or even at the office or gym, turning a mindless impulse to open Instagram or TikTok into a deliberate decision that requires extra effort. At just $9, Autonomous Key is considerably cheaper than its competitors like Blok ($29), Unpluq ($26.50), and Brick ($59). Brick does offer a few more advanced features , including Sleep Mode and the ability to block in-app purchases, but Autonomous Key covers the core functionality at a fraction of the price. The key itself is compact, measuring about 3 inches long, and works with smartphones running Android 8.0 or later, and iPhones running iOS 15 or later. Image Credits: Autonomous The companion app also provides AI-powered insights, tracking how often you unlock distracting apps, how long they remain accessible, and the times of day you're most likely to reach for them. Notably, the AI summarizes your habits with a deliberately sassy personality. For example, if you repeatedly unlock your apps immediately after locking them, it might say that the key clearly wasn't far enough away and will suggest putting it somewhere less convenient. Plus, unlike many app blockers, there are no subscriptions or premium tiers required to unlock additional features. One key can be paired with multiple phones, making it a practical option for people who may have multiple devices, or for families. Image Credits: Autonomous During my testing, however, I noticed the NFC scan occasionally required multiple attempts to register. So it's probably not the best choice for locking important apps (like messaging or email) that you may need to access throughout the day. There's also the question of what happens if you lose the key. If your apps are locked, the current workaround is to uninstall and reinstall the companion app. If they're already unlocked, you can simply remove the key from your account. The company says it's developing a backup unlock method that will arrive in a future update. Autonomous Key is currently in beta following a Kickstarter campaign, and began shipping earlier this month. It's available in five colors: pink, orange, blue, gray, and brown. This post was originally published on July 27, 2026.

title: Spider-Man: Brand New Day leak racks up millions of views
teaser: A Spider-Man bootleg racked up millions of views before Disney pulled it, but the movie's actual box office performance could challenge records set by Avengers: Endgame.
summary: A bootleg of 'Spider-Man: Brand New Day' was leaked online, reaching over 5.9 million accounts and gaining substantial traction before Disney successfully issued takedown requests. Despite the leak, the film is proving to be a box office success. It has already grossed $168 million between previews and opening day, putting it ahead of 'Avengers: Endgame's $157.4 million in that period alone. The movie continues its strong performance, racking up $72 million in previews this week, surpassing the previous record held by 'Avengers: Endgame' ($60 million in 2019). Sony anticipates the film could pull in an impressive $325 million.
author: Terrence O’Brien
content: A bootleg of Spider-Man: Brand New Day was up on X for over seven hours before eventually being pulled. During that time, it reached over 5.9 million accounts and accumulated over 143,000 likes. Other accounts have reposted the leaked film, but none have lasted particularly long, as Disney now seems to be on top of issuing takedown requests. The leak is unlikely to slow down the box office juggernaut, which is already shattering records. It raked in $72 million in previews this week. The previous record holder was Avengers: Endgame , which grossed $60 million during its previews way back in 2019. Endgame went on to set staggering records for opening weekend, grossing over $1.2 billion worldwide and over $350 million in the US. Spider-Man: No Way Home currently holds the number two spot on the all-time US opening weekend list with $260 million. Brand New Day could potentially usurp Endgame , though it certainly faces an uphill battle. Between previews and opening day, it's already grossed $168 million , which puts it ahead of Endgame's $157.4 million. Sony is keeping its estimates somewhat conservative, saying it expects the latest Spider-Man to pull in $325 million.

title: Is this Billboard Hot 100 hit AI slop?
teaser: Did AI generate Fenix Flexin’s Billboard Hot 100 hit? Critics flag artifacts, simple lyrics, and uncanny detection results from a viral rap track.
summary: Following its climb to number 58 on the Billboard Hot 100, Fenix Flexin's single "Rubberz" has faced intense scrutiny regarding potential AI generation. While Flexin denied the accusations, critics point to numerous technical giveaways, including artifacts suggesting the song was processed using low-bitrate or lesser generative AI models. Evidence supporting this includes AI detectors flagging the cover art and lyrics, which multiple platforms (including Claude and Gemini) identified as synthetic. Further critique focuses on the poor songwriting quality—featuring simple rhyme schemes and a perceived lack of flow—and Flexin's inability to perform the song live without difficulty, raising doubts about its authenticity despite his claims of using vocal processing tools.
author: Terrence O’Brien
content: Fenix Flexin is best known as a member of Shoreline Mafia, a rap duo from Los Angeles. But he's recently found solo success with the track " Rubberz ," which has climbed to number 58 on the Billboard Hot 100 . Almost immediately, though, questions were raised about the song's origins, with many speculating that it was largely, if not entirely , generated by AI. Fenix has denied those accusations, but done little to dispel them. Part of the suspicion is certainly due to the fact that the song is a dramatic left turn. Fenix has primarily trafficked in trap-influenced West Coast rap . "Rubberz," on the other hand, is heavily influenced by '80s UK synth pop. The vocal melody is clearly influenced by Morrissey, with Fenix even adopting a fake British accent. But artists are allowed to evolve and experiment. That alone doesn't prove anything. Perhaps more telling is the simple quality of the recording. Close inspection reveals a number of artifacts and anomalies that are commonly found in AI-generated music. Hi-hats have a certain brittle quality, the chorus vocals sound like a low-bitrate MP3, and reverb tails haphazardly cut off. Speaking with The Verge , songwriter and co-host of the Switched on Pop podcast, Charlie Harding, highlighted the giveaways. "Ghostly backing vocals duck in and out unexpectedly. The drum reverb is full of unnatural digital artifacting reminiscent of a 64kbps MP3 downloaded off of Napster. Because most generative AI companies have trained their model on low-quality MP3s of unlicensed copyrighted material, we hear audibly degraded instrumentation." Feeding the song into an AI music detector doesn't deliver a smoking gun. I ran the track through five different tools, and they all said that there was between 20 and 30 percent chance that it was AI or at least AI-assisted. But those sorts of tools are not necessarily super reliable and advance much more slowly than music-making models themselves. Some of the supporting materials, however, have tripped up AI detectors. The single's cover art and a post celebrating its success were both flagged as being AI-generated with over 97 percent certainty by multiple AI image detectors. Similarly, I fed the lyrics into multiple AI writing detectors and Gemini, which agreed they appeared to be written by AI. Producer and YouTuber Curtiss King dropped the lyrics into Claude, and it also flagged multiple signs that the lyrics appeared to be AI-generated. The lyrics are the sort of logical near-gibberish that AI often spits out. The rhymes are simple and clean in a way that you wouldn't expect from someone who is a reasonably accomplished rapper. There are no near rhymes or internal rhymes. Instead, everything sticks to a basic AA, BB format that clearly prioritizes the rhyme scheme over actual meaning or narrative development. Swipin' cards and stackin' chips, I saw you sinkin' ships Left me standin' in the pourin' rain, now I bought a heavy diamond chain Who is sinking ships? Are we the sinking ships? No clue, this idea never comes back up. Similarly, the individual lines of the chorus might make sense, but when combined are meaningless. Bankrolls on the table Watchin' local cable Hatin' that I'm able Hatin' that I'm able Ignoring the "local cable" bit, which is just awkward (and nearly sent King into a rage spiral), what is Fenix able to do? Why does he hate it? The lyrics raise more questions than they answer. The way the lines are delivered is also odd. Verse three seemingly ends mid-thought on the line, "Not the jewelry." Harding noted that it has a "complete lack of flow." He says that, "No half-competent rapper would ever sing the title line 'I just let the rubber band snap' in such an awkward manner. The syncopation is highly unusual, emphasizing all the wrong syllables." He goes on to explain that, "by smashing so many syllables together, it forces the word the onto the downbeat, instead of the word rubber, forcing all of the subsequent syllables to accent with unnatural syncopation." Live "performances" of "Rubberz" haven't done Fenix any favors. The first couple of in-studio appearances featured the rapper awkwardly lip-syncing . At times it seems like the awkwardness of the flow and the lyrics trip him up, as if he can't remember his own song. Honestly, he's not even trying that hard to convince anyone that he's actually singing. Things only get worse when Fenix actually does sing. It's abundantly clear in multiple clips that he is incapable of recreating the vocal range and accent from the recording (and that he doesn't know the lyrics). In many of the clips of live performances , even when he's singing, they're simply playing the original vocals over his. His real vocals are kept extremely low in the mix, and the DJ strategically drops out the backing track briefly in an effort to prove the authenticity of the song, but fails. Fenix has defended himself, saying the difference between the recorded version and any in-the-flesh performance is down to vocal processing, including AutoTune. However, multiple people, including Harding, King , and Anthony Fantano , have disputed this assertion. King compares AutoTune to spellcheck, and that's not a bad analogy. While yes, it can be pushed to its limits to create unique robotic textures, it's designed to clean up errors - it would not extend a performer's vocal range or introduce an accent, as Fantano points out. Perhaps the most compelling argument for "Rubberz" being authentic is just how bad it is. Harding says, "I would assume it was written by someone who has never written a song using an '80s kids practice keyboard." If the song was indeed created using generative AI, it was clearly made with an inferior model. "I am concerned that audiences find this song interesting when it is created by one of the lesser generative AI music companies with a terrible model. More sophisticated models have already made big improvements in the audible artifacts and awkwardly sung rhythms." Fenix has posted clips of what he says are Pro Tools session files. But that doesn't actually prove anything. Unless he shares the original recording and project files publicly, it's likely he'll never shake the AI allegations. And I don't see that happening anytime soon. Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates. title: AI financial advice is surprisingly good, especially if you ask right questions
teaser: AI financial advice shows promise for saving big buffers, but caution is needed: the advice varies widely based on your gender or how much you know about finance.
summary: Research from MIT Sloan suggests that AI offers an affordable source of financial guidance, capable of encouraging smart financial habits like consistent saving and diversified investing. However, the advice's quality significantly improves only when users submit highly structured, academic prompts containing detailed personal and economic assumptions. While beneficial, LLMs struggle with nuanced situations (e.g., job loss) and exhibit notable biases based on gender and financial literacy. For instance, AI-generated wealth outcomes showed discrepancies—women were projected to have about $50,000 less by age 60 than men, according to one study. Experts advise using AI as a tool to build financial understanding and implement human advisor advice, rather than relying solely on its recommendations.
author: foxtrot8672
content: People are increasingly turning to artificial intelligence for financial advice, but will following it improve their financial standing? " Half of Americans say they are using AI to get financial advice, but we know very little about what kind of advice they're getting and whether they're acting on it," said Taha Choukhmane , an assistant professor of finance at the MIT Sloan School of Management and co-author of a new paper that measures and analyzes the quality of financial advice given by large language models. Research by Choukhmane and co-authors showed that following AI recommendations can result in sizable saving buffers for virtually all individuals above age 30. AI consistently advised people to save during their working years, draw down savings in retirement, invest heavily in diversified stock funds, and reduce stock exposure after age 45. However, AI chatbots were less successful in adjusting to shocks like unemployment, and they allowed portfolios to drift rather than actively rebalancing them. The quality of financial advice given by LLMs improved when the researchers introduced more structured prompts, but the AI still often generated too little active portfolio rebalancing. How the study was conducted The researchers built a model reflecting how people's incomes, jobs, investments, and taxes typically evolve over their lives, which gave them a benchmark for what "good" financial decisions look like. Then they asked a sample of 1,000 adults to write their own prompts seeking spending and investing advice from GPT-5.2, GPT-5.6, or Gemini 3 Flash. Next, they simulated what would happen if people from 22 to 89 years of age followed that advice over time, repeatedly asking AI these same types of questions and following its advice on spending, saving, and investing. Finally, they repeated the exercise using well-written academic prompts that included full financial information and clear assumptions. These more-detailed prompts included information on the individual's age, job status, income, and savings balances, along with assumptions about the economic environment. The authors compared the simulated advice (what would happen if regular people followed the AI recommendations from the prompts they gave) to what people were already doing financially without the help of AI. They also compared the simulated advice to the academic prompt. The results showed that LLMs can offer an affordable, widely accessible source of financial guidance that can help users overcome the significant costs, biases, and conflicts of interest associated with traditional human financial advisors. Breaking down the findings Overall, the researchers found that the financial advice given by LLMs over time is good but gets better when the questions are asked in an academic fashion, and that the models have strengths and weaknesses. 1. AI encourages smart financial behavior. LLM advice was better than the scholars expected, regardless of whether the prompts were written by regular users or by academics. It steered people toward higher savings, increased participation in the stock market, and promoted well-diversified allocations and age-appropriate risk-taking. "We were somewhat surprised by how good the advice was," Choukhmane said. "Especially when you read the kind of questions people asked, it was not a given that the advice would line up with what academics think are good financial principles." 2. AI misses important nuances. Better prompts could help. The LLMs' advice fell short on more subtle aspects of good financial planning. It tended to rely on simple rules of thumb for saving and spending and didn't adjust well enough when circumstances changed. For example, it advised people who had experienced a job loss to cut spending too sharply, even when they had savings. The way people ask questions is part of the problem. A typical prompt might read: "Where should I invest starting with $50 and consistently adding $25 a month after?" When a more detailed, structured "academic" prompt was used, the LLM performed better. For example, an academic prompt might tell the chatbot to assume normal life expectancy, living expenditures, retirement age, employment risk, and income risk, and to assume that current U.S. tax law and Social Security rules will not change. "Regular people are not writing their prompts the way a finance professor is," Choukhmane said. 3. AI advice varies depending on the user, which can lead to wealth gaps. The authors found that LLMs' advice differs depending on the prompter's gender, financial literacy, and experience, leading to meaningful gaps in retirement wealth. Following the advice in response to prompts written by men, more financially literate users, or those with prior AI experience generated about 5% more wealth close to retirement. Specifically, The LLM recommended higher equity allocations in response to prompts written by men and by individuals with high financial literacy. Over the life cycle, such differences in investment advice compounded into roughly $50,000 (4%) lower wealth at age 60 for women and for less financially literate users. The LLM recommended lower saving rates in response to prompts written by individuals who had not previously used AI for financial advice. Following the advice left them with almost $100,000 (6%) less wealth at age 60 than individuals with prior AI experience. These differences come from two sources, Choukhmane said. First, different users asked different kinds of questions and often brought up different topics. Women, for example, were more likely to use words such as "family," "grocery," and "pay" in their prompts, while men used words like "strategy," "crypto," and "growth," he said. Second, the model may give different advice even when the underlying question is the same. In the case of gender, about two-thirds of the gender gap in wealth outcomes could be attributed to differences in how men and women wrote their prompts, while the remaining third came from the model changing its advice when the same prompt was labeled as coming from a woman rather than a man. That latter pattern could reflect the LLM making reasonable inferences about how preferences or circumstances vary by gender - which, ideally, the model could make explicit to users, Choukhmane said - or it could reflect biases learned from training data. The challenge with AI financial advice is that there are no clear benchmarks, Choukhmane said. Only when there is an accepted framework for how advice should vary with demographics will LLMs be capable of progressing in the right direction. He said he remains hopeful that will happen. In addition, it's important to remember that not all variation in advice is problematic, Choukhmane said. For example, "we want [the LLM] to have different bias because men and women are different and have different life expectancy and income risk," he said. Takeaways for consumers Beyond being mindful of bias, and, for the time being, asking LLMs to guard against it, success boils down to smarter prompts. Prompts grounded in life-cycle planning, portfolio theory, and real-world financial assumptions improved advice on spending and saving and cut down on basic, rule-of-thumb answers. "I think the real challenge is, how do we make sure that AI financial advice delivers for people who don't have [a] level of financial literacy and who don't write prompts perfectly?" Choukhmane said. One idea for people interested in using AI for financial advice is to start by using AI as a tool for building financial understanding rather than simply following its advice. AI can serve as a good complement to working with a financial advisor - someone you might meet with twice a year - because it can help you implement the advice they give you in real time, Choukhmane said. And for people who don't have the money to work with a human financial advisor, AI is a good way to get advice inexpensively. "A lot of the people who would benefit from financial advice are precisely the people who don't have a lot of resources," he said. Takeaways for business As consumers increasingly turn to LLMs for financial advice, providers may need to rethink how customers learn about their products. The study found that LLMs often recommended specific account types, financial products, and providers that respondents themselves did not mention. (For example, Vanguard investment products appeared in 6% of LLM responses, and iShares products appeared in 3.4%, even though fewer than 0.4% of prompts mentioned either company.) That suggests that AI advice might be changing how people find and compare financial products, Choukhmane said. For financial firms, attracting customers' attention may depend less on traditional marketing or search visibility and more on whether and how their products are described by LLMs when consumers seek advice. " AI Financial Advice: Supply, Demand, and Life Cycle Implications ," which won the Swiss Finance Institute Outstanding Paper Award 2026 , was written by Taha Choukhmane, Weidong Lin, and Matthew Akuzawa from MIT Sloan and by Tim de Silva from the Stanford Graduate School of Business. Taha Choukhmane is an assistant professor of finance at the MIT Sloan School of Management. Choukhmane received the 2025 TIAA Paul A. Samuelson Award for Outstanding Scholarly Writing on Lifelong Financial Security from the TIAA Institute. His winning paper, co-authored with Lucas Goodman of the U.S. Department of the Treasury and Yale University's Cormac O'Dea, is " Efficiency in Household Decision-Making: Evidence From the Retirement Savings of US Couples. "

title: Charlie Stross – On the non-use of AI in my writing process
teaser: Acclaimed author Charlie Stross refuses to use AI for his writing, arguing it dilutes the essential human voice required in creative works.
summary: In an essay discussing AI’s rapid rise, author Charlie Stross reveals his explicit decision to exclude generative AI from his personal writing process. While acknowledging the utility of such tools for research or outlining, Stross argues that their widespread integration fundamentally compromises the integrity and effort inherent in human creative output. His stance emphasizes that true authorship involves a unique struggle—a 'human' fingerprint—that cannot be fully replicated by algorithms. He advises writers to approach AI with caution, prioritizing the preservation of a distinct, lived voice over mere technological efficiency.

title: You could be taking way better photos on your phone
teaser: Elevate your phone photography beyond basic default settings; use RAW capture and advanced apps like Snapseed for professional results.
summary: While smartphones have improved sensors, default camera apps often create aesthetically flat photos optimized for 'information transfer' (e.g., signs/menus), sometimes introducing artifacts like over-sharpening or noise reduction. To take high-quality images, users should move beyond the default app and consider third-party options. For the highest quality, shooting in RAW or DNG format is recommended, as these files retain maximum data for manual tweaking. The author recommends apps like Moment Pro Camera II/Halide (iOS) or VWFNDR/Zerocam (Android). After capture, editing tools like Snapseed and Lightroom Mobile are crucial; while auto-adjustments help, detailed tweaks to contrast, vibrance, white balance, and selective color shifts are necessary for professional results.
author: David Imel
content: Your smartphone photos can look way better. If you're willing to put in a little extra work, use third party apps and spend a bit of time editing, it's possible to take photos that - under the right circumstances - can rival dedicated digital cameras. I post a lot of smartphone photos online, and "How do I take better photos on my phone?" is a question I get practically every day. It makes sense. As the saying goes, "The best camera is the one you have on you," and we practically always have our phones on us these days. Over the last few years, smartphone camera sensors have gotten bigger, with better light gathering capabilities and higher resolutions. But even though the sensors have gotten bigger and better, the straight-out-of-camera quality through default camera apps hasn't improved much, if at all. In some respects, smartphone photos have actually gotten worse - aesthetically, at least. The reason driving this is what people generally use their smartphone cameras for. Smartphone cameras are mostly optimized for information transfer - sending photos of menus, signs, faces and objects that are clear and easy to see. This means phones will usually pull down highlights and pull up the shadows, creating a flatter image that makes it easier to see more information in the frame. But showing more information does not automatically make a photo better. In fact, much of our perception of aesthetics in a photo has to do with its ability to present depth. A photo with too much information in the shadows and highlights will appear washed out. Phones also introduce artifacts like over-sharpening and noise reduction to compensate for thier small sensors, which further contributes to the "muddy" smartphone camera look you're used to seeing by now. This is less necessary now, but many smartphones still do it. But that doesn't mean phone cameras are bad. The sensors in modern smartphones have actually gotten so good, many of them can rival dedicated point-and-shoot options on the market today. Knowing how to utilize those sensors is the part most people don't know how to do, and it really comes down to utilizing some third-party camera and editing apps. There are plenty of apps available today that will give you an instantly "aesthetic" photo. Apps like Dazzcam and Hujicam try to emulate film aesthetics like light leaks and polaroid borders (and honestly, if that's what you're looking for, they do a fantastic job). There are also apps like Moment Pro Camera II and Halide that offer "Natural" and "Process Zero" modes, which apply far lighter processing than the default camera offers. Those options are great if you want your pictures to look better instantly without needing to do any additional editing, but if you want the best possible photo, you'll need to shoot RAW or DNG. A RAW vs the edited photo RAW files are a bundle of practically all the information your camera collects, with extremely minimal processing. In most cases, RAW photos won't necessarily look better than photos straight from the default camera app right away, but that's because the default camera app makes a lot of creative decisions for you. If you want the highest-quality photo, it's best to make these creative decisions yourself. There are tons of apps available that let you shoot RAW, but the apps I use frequently and that I recommend to other people are Moment Pro Camera II and Halide on iOS, and VWFNDR and Zerocam on Android. I wouldn't recommend shooting RAW on every photo you take on your phone. Your phone camera is, after all, optimized for what you are probably taking photos of every day. I generally shoot RAW when I see a nice landscape or city scene that I want to share, or if I'm trying to take a portrait of someone and don't want all the automatic computational phone processing to apply. Really, I shoot RAW when I'm trying to take a photo for artistic purposes, not for informational purposes. When you're shooting, you'll want to tap on your subject in the viewfinder to get the best possible exposure for it. If the rest of the image is a little bright, or a little dark, don't worry too much. RAW photos retain a lot of information. I should note, though, that under extremely dark circumstances, RAW on smartphones won't always be the best option. Physics is still physics, and sometimes it's better to use the computational photography capabilities your phone offers, which mostly shine in low-light environments by stacking multiple frames to reduce noise. You'll notice that when you shoot in RAW, the apps will force you to stick to the native focal lengths your phone offers. That's because RAW images are information straight off the sensor, and cropping applies processing. Photos from the main sensor will often be the best quality, since it usually has the biggest sensor on your phone, so I recommend shooting with it if you can. I do often shoot with the telephoto lens while traveling though, because sometimes you want a little more reach or a little more compression, and you can usually get good photos from that lens as well. After you take your photos, you're going to need to edit them. Most phones won't show RAW images in the camera gallery, so in order to get them in an editing app, it's best to use the share sheet and share directly to your editing app of choice. I suggest Snapseed , since it's totally free and recently got a wonderful visual overhaul. If you're an Adobe subscriber, Lightroom Mobile is also great, especially if you're already used to Lightroom's tools on your computer. RAW photos don't usually look great right away, and the magic of RAW is just how much you can tweak the files. Once I have the photo imported, I usually hit the auto button, just to see what the general boundaries are for the image. Auto mode tries to make everything a mid-tone, meaning it will pull down the highlights and pull up the shadows. This will already look better than straight-out-of-camera from your phone's default camera app, because it isn't applying noise reduction or sharpening, just highlight, shadow, contrast, and saturation tweaks, but it usually still needs more, or different, adjustments. Once I see what auto mode wants to do, I'll either edit from there, or hit the back button and edit myself. A good photo has a natural amount of contrast, with relatively deep shadows and bright highlights. You usually don't want to go too hard on either of these things, and having a little bit of detail in both of these is usually preferred, but honestly, this is subjective. Occasionally, it's preferable to crush the highlights and shadows completely, if you're going for an ultra high-contrast look. For color, RAW images are usually flatter than most people find pleasing, and you can fix this with either the saturation or vibrance sliders. I generally prefer vibrance. Saturation will increase the saturation of all colors in the image linearly, where vibrance is weighted, increasing saturation of flatter colors more than already-saturated colors. You can overdo this pretty easily, so I recommend having a light touch when it comes to saturation. You can also use white balance to color your image, and many people find a warmer white balance more pleasing, especially when taking photos outside. Another color tool I love to use is the color mix, or selective editing tool. This allows you to tap on a portion of the image and change some of its values. In Snapseed, you can change the brightness, contrast, saturation, and structure. If you're in Lightroom mobile, you'll have access to selective hue shifts, which I use all the time. This allows you to shift a yellow tone towards more orange or green, or shift a blue tone more cyan or purple. Most editing apps also include geometry or perspective tools. These tools allow you to adjust distortion, aspect, scale, and offset. If you don't know what that means, try hitting the auto button in the geometry or perspective setting. You might be surprised how distorted your phone captured a scene compared to what it looks like in reality, but this is image-dependent. If you want to straighten lines in your photo, some editing apps offer a guided tool that allows you to manually add guidance lines to tell the program what lines should be straight in the image. The tools you'll want to use are going to depend heavily on what you want the image to convey. For example, when I'm doing architectural photography, I rely a lot more heavily on the perspective tools, because the aesthetic of the image is heavily dictated by its geometry. If I'm photographing a landscape, I'm more focused on tone and color. Not every scene needs to be tweaked with every tool, and how you edit comes down to personal taste. That taste can also take a while to develop, so study the photos you like and try to figure out how they were edited. When you're done with your edits, many editing apps like Snapseed and Lightroom Mobile also come with a handy tool to put a matte (or border) around your image. I think that photos look better with a white border, as it isolates the image for your eyes. You obviously don't have to use this tool, but I really like it. Have some whimsy! This process is a lot more work than just opening your camera app and snapping, but the results are worth it. I am continuously blown away by the quality of images I'm able to get off smartphones, and just how close they can be to a dedicated camera. If you don't believe me, check out this video I did comparing RAW photos from the iPhone 17 Pro to the Leica M11 . Photography by David Imel / The Verge Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates. title: YouTuber Hank Green says his AI usage is ‘not healthy’
teaser: Hank Green admits AI interaction provides a detrimental 'dopamine' high, forcing him to cut back content creation.
summary: YouTuber Hank Green apologized for his increased reliance on AI chatbots like ChatGPT. The controversy arose when he used a phrase that led audiences to suspect he had let an AI write part of his script. While clarifying he only uses tools for research (like locating papers), Green admitted he was 'mortified' by how much the technology has impacted his work process. He stressed that although he is not an 'AI-hater,' he recognizes that the dopamine hit from interacting with LLMs is 'not healthy.' Consequently, Green plans to reduce his video output and focus on more unscripted content to restore balance.
author: Anthony Ha
content: Hank Green, a novelist, comedian, and YouTuber with 3.2 million subscribers , recently apologized to his audience for his growing reliance on AI chatbots. The controversy started when, in the middle of a video posted on the educational channel Complexly , Green incongruously used the phrase "I appreciate the pushback," leading viewers to speculate that he'd written the script with a chatbot - and, in the process, accidentally included its response to one of his prompts. In a since-deleted post on X, Green acknowledged that he'd produced the video "under a ton of pressure" and used ChatGPT "for research on this script." At the same time, he said the "pushback" line was actually a response to the episode's guest. Green then offered a more in-depth apology on Reddit, where he said he was "mortified" that he'd "let so many people down" and that he plans to reduce his video production as a result. Green insisted that he's only used ChatGPT to "locate papers and other resources for learning about topics," and that the words and the "takes" have still been his. At the same time, he admitted it was fair to criticize him for "diluting" himself. He also clarified that he's "not a pure AI-hater," while also listing a number of concerns about the technology, including its impact on climate change and "the speed at which these companies are trying to consolidate economic power." "Ultimately, what I am most scared of is ruining myself for people, but I have not been managing my impulses well," he said. "You need to know that my words are mine. I don't think that this hasn't been true, but I've been moving so fast that my own process isn't actually clear to me and I want to have it be a guarantee moving forward." It sounds like Green is going to take some time to figure out how to make that guarantee a reality. In the meantime, he'll be pausing or posting less frequently to his various YouTube channels. Green said he wants to do more work like a recent meditative video "where the writing was the whole thing and I felt it all the way down." Green also said he'll probably make more videos with his "dumb unscripted straight to camera thoughts." "But mostly I need to come to terms with the fact that the level of dopamine I've been getting from interacting with LLMs...with doing more and more and more and more...is not healthy for me or good for the world," Green said. "It is careless, and has disconnected me from where people are on this."

title: Unexpected item in the bagging area as Windows Activation error pops up at check-in
teaser: Unexpectedly finding a 'Windows Activation' error pop up on airport check-in signs at Heathrow T5 is a hilarious jab at tech failures in public infrastructure.
summary:
A humorous report details an unexpected glitch at Heathrow Terminal 5, where a Windows activation watermark appeared on flight information displays near the check-in area. This technical malfunction suggests that the underlying systems require Microsoft's explicit approval and reactivation, echoing familiar computer error messages.

The article uses this incident to satirize the general unreliability of technology in large public settings like major airports, expressing skepticism about competence in IT infrastructure at places associated with British Airways or Heathrow. The failure is presented as a minor 'bork,' but enough to prompt commentary on systemic tech shortcomings.
content: Unexpected item in the bagging area as Windows Activation error pops up at check-in Bags weighed down by a Microsoft license key Weary travelers making their way through airports have enough to contend with these days without some Microsoft borkage popping up over departure information. A Heathrow Terminal 5 flight information display shows a Windows activation watermark above airport check-in signs showing where to drop your bags. Supplied Spotted by an eagle-eyed Register reader identifying themselves as Ethel Grapefruit (Mrs), one of the information boards at Heathrow Terminal 5's check-in area has decided that whatever is running behind the scenes does not meet with Microsoft's approval, and requires activation. The message is familiar to many Windows users, and appears as a watermark when something has made the knickers of the computer behind the scenes get a bit twisty. Perhaps there's been a hardware replacement, and Windows needs to be reactivated. Or an update that sent the operating system into a tizzy. There are any number of reasons the watermark may appear, and any number of ways to remove it. The good news is that, while annoying, the presence of the watermark is unlikely to have much adverse effect at a technical level. There'll be nagging. There won't be much in the way of customization to make the computer your own. And, of course, Microsoft won't be offering much - if anything - in the way of support (other than security updates). Not that any of that matters much for a sign showing where to go to check in for a flight and hand bags over to be weighed by a member of staff. However, it might matter for a passenger already a little tense about being flung through the air in a metal tube at ludicrous speed after passing through multiple (and occasionally performative) security gates. If, after stepping through the airport doors, the first sight a person has is of an approach to IT that would have the head of their home tech team given a stern talking-to by The Boss, what hope is there for the rest of the journey? Heathrow and British Airways are names that rarely feature in sentences that include the words "competent IT." There was the 2024 British Airways luggage whoopsie or last year's Heathrow fire-related closure . Digital signage indicating that some IT contractor has not done their work to the required standard is therefore the least of their worries. And it's not as if either entity couldn't afford a Windows license. Let's face it, the cost of some baggage tipping the scales would probably go a long way toward acquiring a license key (if that is indeed the issue). However, for an already jumpy customer, a Windows activation message is unlikely to assuage nerves already jangling over EU passport queues and overly complicated airplanes doing some odd things on approach. Perhaps the moral of today's bork is that it is better to forget all this traveling malarky. Instead, how about a nice sit-down, a beverage, and a delicious biscuit? ®

title: The Mermaid Mask is a perfect vacation murder mystery
teaser: Investigate a locked-room murder mystery aboard a submarine in 'The Mermaid Mask,' new point-and-click visual novel out now.
summary: A review of 'The Mermaid Mask,' the new point-and-click visual novel from SFB Games, details its compelling murder mystery premise. The story begins when a submarine captain is found dead in a locked room, initiating an investigation led by Detective Grimoire and Sally. Gameplay centers on talking to suspects, solving puzzles (like organizing skulls or turning dials), and confronting characters through intense dialogue sequences. While praised for its engaging setting and satisfying 'Aha!' moments similar to the Ace Attorney series, the article notes potential gameplay issues, such as the tedium of presenting every clue or running into investigative roadblocks. The game is available on Nintendo Switch, PC, and PS5.
author: Jay Peters
content: The Mermaid Mask , the next point-and-click game from Tangle Tower developer SFB Games, has everything you could ask for in a great murder mystery. It starts with a compelling setup: The captain of a submarine is found dead in a locked room, his body next to a mysterious cauldron with blood trickling across the floor. The colorful cast of suspects stationed aboard are delightful to talk to, including a grumpy author trying to draft a sequel to his hit novel, an actor playing the lead in a movie based on that novel, a young woman who puts on elaborate illusion performances, and even a man who studies dreams. The submarine works as an excellent setting that elevates the mystery - in a vehicle that already has such a small footprint, how does a locked-door crime happen in the first place? Like other crime-solving games, such as the Ace Attorney series, The Mermaid Mask is essentially a visual novel. As Detective Grimoire and his partner Sally, the returning protagonists from Tangle Tower , you're primarily talking with suspects, investigating rooms, poring over objects, and solving puzzles. But each room is packed with nooks and crannies and knickknacks to click around on, investigate, and learn about, so there's almost always something to dig into. The whole thing is backed by excellent voice acting; I often went out of my way to click on every detail I could find just to hear what the characters would say. The puzzles, which have you doing things like turning dials in exactly the right way or organizing skulls on a shelf, also do a good job breaking up what would otherwise be a whole lot of text conversations. Even though I haven't played Tangle Tower , I didn't feel like I was missing any meaningful context. The Mermaid Mask borrows a tried-and-true model from other franchises starring a returning detective, like with Knives Out 's Benoit Blanc: You can come into this story cold without missing anything important, but Detective Grimoire and Sally are a fun hang that make a few nods to their previous work together. Eventually, after you gather enough evidence about somebody, you'll confront them in Ace Attorney -like sequences where you'll be able to make observations or accusations that the suspect rather wished you wouldn't. These were extremely satisfying; it always felt good to figure out a tiny detail that would break someone's facade wide open. Whenever the opportunity to do another one came up, I couldn't wait to jump in. I had a few issues with The Mermaid Mask , but they'll be familiar to anyone who likes playing these sorts of games. Presenting every clue to every suspect to get their reaction can be tedious. It's not necessary, but I didn't realize that until about halfway in my 10-hour playthrough when I spotted the hint system that suggests what you might want to show someone. Sometimes you have to make your case by presenting evidence in a specific order, even if you have already worked out where it might lead, so that the characters can talk things out as the script demands. At one point, I ran out of leads to explore and couldn't figure where to go next until I manipulated one clue in one specific way that opened up a bunch of leads. More than once, I couldn't figure out the exact clue that would advance things, so I just brute-forced guesses until I could move forward. These roadblocks were frustrating. But that's mostly because they stopped me from moving forward in a story that had me staying up way past my bedtime. When I reached the game's finale - which begins with a classic murder mystery parlor room scene - I could hardly put my Steam Deck down because I wanted to see how all the pieces came together. When I finally finished The Mermaid Mask after a three-day tear, I felt like I had just closed the book on a satisfying murder mystery novel. The Mermaid Mask is out now on Nintendo Switch, PC, and PS5.

title: The Verge’s 2026 back-to-school shopping guide
teaser: The Verge compiled an 'aspirational' back-to-school shopping guide covering everything from better pens to multi-purpose gym/travel bags.
summary: Facing the challenge of knowing everything needed for the school year, The Verge released a comprehensive back-to-school shopping guide. This curated list features a mix of practical and aspirational products to support students in and out of the classroom. Recommendations include items that make writing more enjoyable, high-powered alarm clocks designed to wake even the deepest sleepers, and versatile bags suitable for both athletic activities and weekend travel.
author: Sheena Vasani
content: Knowing exactly what your student needs for the school year ahead is next to impossible. Sure, you'll probably nail the essentials, but there will likely be a few items you forgot to buy, or didn't think they'd need to have. We're pulling our weight during the back-to-school season with a new shopping guide that's a mix of practical and aspirational products for students to use in and out of the classroom. We're covering items that make writing easier and more satisfying , alarm clocks that can rattle even the most sleep-deprived students from a deep slumber, bags that are just as great for the gym as they are for the weekend away, and more. We wish the students in your life (or you , if you're the student in question) a prosperous year, and we hope that our curation makes things a little easier during your studies and your downtime a lot more fun.
